newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO, Israel resume recriminations, await Albright.
newsitem.headline: PLO, Israel resume recriminations, await Albright.

text.p: Palestinians and Israelis resumed their recrimination on Thursday a day after a U.S. mediator completed a peace mission with only partial results.
The two sides looked to U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to salvage peacemaking. Her spokesman said on Thursday she would definitely travel to the Middle East in August or September.
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross's mission was spurred by a July 30 suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market that killed 16 people, including the attackers.
He said before leaving the area on Wednesday that his success in getting Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security officials talking was a start in restoring security links.
But remarks by officials on both sides conveyed a severe crisis in trust.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat charged on Thursday that Israel was not ready to work to save peace deals signed since 1993.
"How can you dance the tango alone? You need a partner who is ready to dance with you," Arafat told reporters after meeting Israeli peace activists and left-wing lawmakers in Ramallah.
"We say, 'Is this government really ready to work with us to preserve the eace process and protect it? Is it really ready to do so?' I am sorry to say the answer is no," he said.

Arafat assailed Israeli sanctions imposed after the twin bombing, including a closure of the West Bank and Gaza Strip which has prevented tens of thousands of Palestinians from reaching their jobs in Israel.
Israel says it will not lift the closure or transfer tax and customs revenue it owes the Palestinians until Arafat cracks down on Islamic militants.
The Israeli army said it had lifted its siege, or "internal closure", of Hebron and Ramallah but the town of Bethlehem and an area surrounding Jerusalem remained sealed off.
"The ball is now in the Americans' court," Palestinian Cabinet Secretary Ahmed Abdel-Rahman told Reuters.
A senior U.S. official on Thursday told reporters he hoped Israel would make the financial transfers it owed the Palestinians once Arafat took action against militants.
"Measures that are taken that are punitive in nature ...holding up the money, is something that we think is not a good idea," he added, speaking on condition he not be named.
Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan, speaking before Arafat's comments, said Israel had yet to see Arafat act.
"We don't see anything really concrete. We see a certain seriousness in their meetings with us and we welcome it. We are waiting to see if it translates into deeds," he told Reuters.

Albright's trip was expected to focus on reviving substantive negotiations frozen since Netanyahu broke ground last March at Har Homa, a Jewish settlement on a hill in Arab East Jerusalem known as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Albright has said it was essential that Arafat make a "100 percent effort" to prevent militant attacks.
Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters Washington had to take charge of peacemaking.
"We simply have a zero trust level with Mr Netanyahu ... which creates the need for a third party intervention," he said.
But Tayeb Abdel Rahim, secretary of the Palestinian Presidency, accused Washington of encouraging Israeli policies that wrecked peacemaking.

"Dennis Ross came and left but let me tell you that the hitherto American attitude encouraged the Israeli government to build a settlement in Jabal Abu Ghneim and to domolish homes," he told graduates of a Palestinian police training course in remarks he attributed to Arafat.
In Hebron, Palestinians said that a boy wounded in clashes with Israeli troops last month died in hospital. In the central West Bank, Israel partly demolished five Arab homes built without permits.
In Jerusalem, an Israeli court sentenced two border policemen to eight months in jail and 12 months suspended for brutalising Palestinians last October.
